## Who he is

**Yiğit Darçın — Director of Engineering, Trendyol Group.** Leads data, ML and core technology, ~750+ engineers. Ex co-founder of Dolap (bought by Trendyol), before that n11.com, Prime Teknoloji, Turkcell Teknoloji. Bilkent CS. Publicly active about Trendyol's eng culture — Go at 1.5M throughput, building an ML *platform* rather than one-off ML projects, running their HackerOne bug bounty. He's a platform-builder and an eng-brand guy, not a procurement buyer.

## The intro context — I couldn't find any

This is the part worth flagging: **there is no written context anywhere I can see.** The cal.com booking carries no notes or agenda field. Nothing in Gmail mentioning him or Trendyol other than marketing mail and unrelated LinkedIn digests. Nothing in Slack. So the intro happened somewhere I can't read — LinkedIn DM, X, WhatsApp, or a warm intro by phone. **Who connected you, and what did you tell him Lobu was?** That single fact changes the whole meeting, and I'd rather ask than guess.

## Brainstorm

**Read the room first.** A director who books a generic 30-min intro slot from a personal address is not running a purchase. Realistically he's in one of four modes: curious about the OSS because his teams are wiring agentic AI right now; scouting for a hire or advisor; sizing you up as a peer; or genuinely has an internal problem. Your first three minutes should find out which — ask him what made him book, before you present anything.

**The wedge that actually fits Trendyol.** They build in-house, they open-source, they have a strong not-invented-here reflex, and they're a Turkish company with data-residency instincts. Any pitch shaped as "send your company data to my cloud" dies on contact. What survives is the opposite: it's open source, you run it on your infra, here's the repo. That's not a concession, it's the reason you get in the door where Glean and Dust can't. Lead with self-hostable.

**The problem statement he'll recognize.** At 750 engineers, every team has independently pointed Claude Code or Codex at their own tools. There's no shared, permission-aware memory of the company — each agent rebuilds context per session and throws it away. That's a *platform* problem, and platform problems are literally his job title. Frame Lobu as the shared context layer under the agents his teams already run, not as another agent product they'd have to adopt.

**Demo, if it gets there.** Thirty minutes means ten minutes of demo maximum. My pick, in order:

1. **Recall from Claude Code** — ask a question in his tool that only lands because Lobu stitched several sources. He's an engineer; this is the one that reads as real rather than as a slide.
2. **`npx @lobu/cli init` → `lobu run` → UI on :8787 with embedded Postgres.** Two minutes, kills the trust objection dead, and gives him something he can hand a staff engineer this week. For this audience I'd almost put it first.
3. **Delegation to a persistent specialist** — good, but it's the thing that most sounds like everyone else's demo. Save it unless he pulls the thread.

I would *not* spend today building a Trendyol-flavored demo org with seller/campaign/incident entities. It's the tempting move, it eats your whole morning, and for an intro call a generic-but-live demo beats a bespoke-but-rehearsed one. Hold that for a second meeting where it's earned.

**Don't overclaim the isolation story.** Your own note on this is unambiguous: the tenant boundary is per-org/per-agent, not per-employee — worker filesystems are `workspaces/{agentId}`. Someone running 750 engineers will ask, and if he catches an overclaim the meeting is over. The honest version is strong enough: org boundary, cross-org runs rejected, workers only ever see `lobu_secret_<uuid>` placeholders and never raw credentials.

**One tension to resolve before you talk.** Your saved GTM note locks the hero as *"Open-source backend for multi-user AI agents"*, but the current README leads with *"shared company context for every AI agent."* Those pull in different directions — backend-you-build-on versus context-layer-you-connect. For this guy the context-layer framing is the better opener, but pick one deliberately in advance instead of drifting between them mid-call.

**Questions worth asking him.** What are his teams doing with agents today, and who owns it. Whether anything runs in production or it's all pilots. Whether "our data leaves our infra" is a hard no. And the one that matters most for you: whether he'd put an engineer on running it for a week. That last one converts a nice chat into a next step.

**The trap.** Per your own kill-criterion note, this kind of meeting is exactly where a pilot ask gets deferred into "let's stay in touch." A flattering conversation with a director at a 750-engineer company will feel like progress whether or not anything happens. Decide now what you're asking for at minute 25 — I'd make it "let me get one of your engineers running it this week," not a purchase.

- Meeting time, link, and booking provenance: **high** — read directly from the cal.com confirmation and cross-checked against the busy block on `emre@lobu.ai`.
- Who Yiğit is: **medium-high** — web sources (Crunchbase, LinkedIn, LeadDev) agree on role and scope; the 750-engineer figure is his own public phrasing, not verified.
- Intro context: **high confidence that none exists in writing** — searched Gmail across Trendyol, his name, and intro/demo threads, plus Slack, all empty. Low confidence about what was actually said, since it happened off-channel.
- Demo advice: **medium** — grounded in your README and saved GTM notes, but I haven't run the demo path myself today.

**Next actions**

1. Tell me who made the intro and what he already knows — I'll retune the opener and the ask around it.
2. Let me do a dry run of `npx @lobu/cli init` → `lobu run` → :8787 now, so you know it's clean on the current build before you screen-share it.
3. Decide the headline you're leading with (context layer vs. backend) and I'll write the 90-second version of it.
4. Pick the minute-25 ask, and I'll draft the follow-up email to send within the hour after the call.

Morning of **Aug 11**, six hours before you asked for the intro:

He was **sitting in a meeting at Trendyol** when he wrote that. The thought was literally "this thing they're describing could be built in Lobu." You replied at 13:08 — *"fraud guzel use-case aynen abi, ekleyeyim websitesine"* — and then at 14:37 asked him for the intro to Yiğit. So the chain is: internal Trendyol fraud project → Umut thinks "that's Lobu" → intro.

## Is Yiğit the one doing it?

Probably adjacent, but that's inference and I want to be clear about the gap. What's established: someone at Trendyol wants to build a basic fraud tool, and Umut — who reports to Yiğit — was in the room. What's *not* established: he said *"istiyorlar"* (they want), never "we" and never named Yiğit. So it could be his own team, a sibling team, or a different org entirely.

The circumstantial case is decent: Yiğit publicly leads data, ML and core technology, and at a marketplace, fraud sits squarely in that stack. But I wouldn't walk in assuming it's his project.

**The cheap fix: just ask Umut before 14:00.** He replies fast, he's already up at this hour on a weekday, and it's a one-line question — is the fraud thing in Yiğit's org, and is it okay to bring it up. That single answer decides whether fraud is your opening or a card you keep in your pocket. Going in and guessing wrong is worse than either.

## If it is his

Then Sardine is the shape of what they'd be comparing against, and that's a good position for you rather than a threat. Trendyol is never buying a US fraud SaaS for the Turkish market — they'll build. Your line isn't "I have a fraud product," it's "I'm not selling you a fraud tool, I'm selling the thing you'd build yours on: connectors into your own data, typed entities, automations with approvals, running on your infra, with an audit trail." Build-vs-buy where you're neither side of the choice — you're the substrate for the build.

content.text:
Read his X and LinkedIn through your own logged-in Chrome. This changed the picture materially.

## The find that matters

His LinkedIn post from **four weeks ago** is about *Turn the Ship Around* (David Marquet) — the nuclear submarine captain who replaced "request permission to submerge" with "I intend to submerge." His summary of the principle: **"bilgiyi yetkiye taşıma, yetkiyi bilginin olduğu yere taşı"** — don't move information up to authority, move authority down to where the information is. He's careful that delegated authority alone isn't enough; it needs competence and clarity alongside it, or "I trust you" just pushes people into a void.

Then he ends the post with this:

> *"Bugün bu mesele daha da kritik. Yalnızca insanlara değil, ajanlara da iş devrediyoruz artık. Devrederken sorduğumuz soru aynı: emir mi veriyoruz, niyet mi? Kontrolü bırakmak gücü bırakmak değil, doğru sorumluluğu doğru yere vermek."*

We're now delegating work not only to people but to agents. The question is the same — are we giving orders, or intent? Letting go of control isn't letting go of power, it's putting the right responsibility in the right place.

He published his own theory of agent delegation a month ago, and it is almost exactly what your approvals, permissions, and audit layer implements. Competence, clarity, authority pushed down, accountability retained. If you open the call anywhere, open there — not with what Lobu is, but with his sentence, and then: *that's the thing I've been building the mechanics for.* You will not get a better hook than a man's own words from four weeks ago.

## Two corrections to what I told you

**The ML-platform framing is his after all.** I was wrong last turn. The LinkedIn *article* is Trendyol Group's byline, but on X (Dec 29) he wrote it himself: *"Bir parçası olmaktan gurur duyduğum ML platform ekibi, Trendyol'da ML'i 'tekil projeler' olmaktan çıkarıp bir platform haline getirdi."* — the ML platform team I'm proud to be part of took ML at Trendyol from "individual projects" to a platform. So the individual-projects-to-platform line is quotable and it's his.

**Drop the "bring a metric" advice.** His post from a month ago on *The Score Takes Care of Itself* cites **Goodhart's Law** by name — the moment a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. He's explicitly scornful of "more code, more deployment, more tokens" and of ticket-count targets. Walsh's Standard of Performance is his model: don't set the number, build the system that produces it. So if you walk in with a KPI you'll land badly. Talk about the system and the behaviour; let the number be a consequence. The 30% in his LeadDev talk is something he reports afterwards, not something he aimed at.

## Where he's actually active

**LinkedIn is the channel** — 6,295 followers, roughly monthly long-form Turkish essays, each one a book he's read applied to engineering leadership. Marquet on delegation, Walsh on standards, Green Book on doing one thing completely. That last one is a plea against multitasking: don't pile parallel work on teams, pick few things, finish them, close them.

**X is dormant** — last post Feb 23, on Chad Fowler's *Relocating Rigor*, where his comment was *"the best transformations don't remove discipline — they relocate rigor closer to feedback, tests, and reality."* Same thesis as the LeadDev talk, one sentence.

**Medium is dead** since Jul 2024.

## Marquet

David Marquet — US Navy captain who took command of the USS Santa Fe, a nuclear submarine that was the worst-performing in its fleet, and turned it into one of the best inside a year. He wrote it up as *Turn the Ship Around!*

The pivotal moment: he'd trained for a whole year on a different submarine and got reassigned at the last minute, so he didn't actually know this boat. One day he gave an order that was impossible on that particular ship — and the crew tried to carry it out anyway. He asked why nobody objected. The answer was one line: **"Because you said so."** He realized he was commanding a culture of yes-men, which on a nuclear submarine isn't just inefficient, it's dangerous.

His fix was a language change. Navy convention is "I request permission to submerge." He banned it and replaced it with **"I intend to submerge."** The point being that to say "I intend," you must already have thought through every justification: *Captain, I intend to submerge. We're in our own waters, depth checked at 400 feet, all personnel below, ship ready to dive.* Captain says "very well." The authority still sits with him — but the thinking has moved down to where the information is.

Marquet's compressed version, which is the line Yiğit quotes: **don't move information up to authority; move authority down to where the information is.** With the caveat that delegated authority alone isn't enough — it needs competence (so delegating is safe) and clarity (so everyone knows the intent). Without all three, "I trust you" just pushes people into a void.

**And here's why it matters for you:** Yiğit wrote all of that on LinkedIn four weeks ago, in Turkish, and then closed the post by extending it to AI — *we're now delegating not only to people but to agents; the question is the same, orders or intent.*

So the opening isn't you citing a management book. It's you saying **"I read your post."** Don't pretend to have read Marquet — if he asks, you've read his post about it, which is true and is the better answer anyway. Referencing someone's own writing beats referencing their favourite author every time.

## On the demo

Good pick, and it's the one that fits every opening. Two things it demands: rehearse the happy path until it's boring, and make the action look real rather than a toy — an agent trying to do something with consequences, hitting the approval, a human deciding, and the whole thing recorded. That sequence *is* "intent not orders" made concrete, which is why it works no matter which opening you choose.

Now that Marquet makes sense, pick the opening.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* — most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token — a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Before publishing, scan the stylesheet for any color declared only inside a media or `[data-theme]` block — that is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject — or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name — a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word — a greeting, a category, a page-type label — the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.
